asset_classes.name: Agency RMBS
asset_classes.how_it_works: Pass-through securities backed by residential mortgages that carry a government or GSE guarantee (Ginnie Mae, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac) against default risk - so unlike every other asset class in this report, credit risk is essentially not the story here. The entire investment case is interest-rate and prepayment risk: when rates fall, homeowners refinance and return principal early (reinvestment risk at lower yields); when rates rise, prepayments slow and duration extends just as rates are moving against you (negative convexity, the defining technical feature of this asset class).
asset_classes.market_size_issuance: MBS issuance reached $337.7B year-to-date through February 2026, up 16.2% y/y; agency MBS trading volume averaged $396.8B daily, up 7.2% y/y - both signal healthy market liquidity and demand.
asset_classes.performance_commentary: Mixed across 2026 so far: the Bloomberg U.S. MBS Index returned +0.07% in April (+0.24% excess return to Treasuries) but -1.42% in July, when sector option-adjusted spread (OAS) widened 7bp to +31bp - a real, sourced spread move, not a proxy. Agency MBS is coming off its best year since 2002 (+8.5% in 2025), and PIMCO's lead portfolio manager describes 2026 valuations as still 'cheap on average' even after that rally.
asset_classes.institutional_commentary: PIMCO (Dan Hyman, managing director): 'We continue to see good opportunities in the agency mortgage in 2026, with valuations on average looking cheap and differentiation of bonds within the market creating good relative value opportunities for active managers' (2026). Separately, PIMCO frames agency MBS as 'an important defensive anchor in the portfolio' given tight corporate spreads elsewhere - a relative-value argument, not an absolute one.
asset_classes.institutional_investment_activity: PIMCO's Total Return Fund and Income Fund both hold ~18% in agency MBS as of June 30, 2026. PIMCO's actively-managed MBS ETF (PMBS, $1.3B AUM) drew over $800M in inflows over the trailing year - a clear signal of institutional/advisor rotation into active MBS management specifically, not just passive exposure.
asset_classes.fed_sensitivity: High and structurally amplified by negative convexity. Agency MBS effective duration runs roughly 5-6 years currently, so a 25bp Fed-driven rate move implies a rough 1.25-1.5% price impact before convexity - but because prepayments slow when rates rise, duration extends further right when you don't want it to, meaning realized losses in a selloff tend to exceed the simple duration math, while gains in a rally are capped by refinancing. The Fed's own balance sheet actions matter directly here too: the Fed cut its Reserve Management Purchases to zero starting August 14, 2026, removing a buyer from the market at the margin.
asset_classes.headwinds_tailwinds: Tailwind: the Trump administration's GSE MBS purchase program (Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac authorized to buy $200B of agency MBS, announced January 8, 2026) tightened spreads and boosted 2026 performance, though PIMCO notes conviction has 'moderated a bit' now that spreads are narrower post-rally. Headwind: continued Fed MBS runoff (holdings fell below $2 trillion by end of Q1 2026) keeps a structural seller/non-buyer in the market with banks 'comparatively inactive,' which is why spreads remain unusually wide by historical standards even with the GSE program's support.
asset_classes.sentiment_outlook: Constructive but not uncomplicated - PIMCO's own framing captures the tension well: cheap on an absolute/relative basis and a genuine defensive anchor, but the spread-widening episode in July 2026 shows the asset class is still exposed to real volatility when technicals (Fed runoff, bank demand) turn unfavorable even without any credit-quality story at all.

asset_classes.name: Non-Agency RMBS
asset_classes.how_it_works: Residential mortgage pools without a government/GSE guarantee - real credit risk, unlike agency RMBS. Deals pool 500-2,000 mortgage loans into senior-subordinate structures, where subordination (junior tranches absorb losses first) and performance triggers insulate senior bondholders from collateral volatility. The largest growth segment is non-QM (non-Qualified Mortgage) - loans to borrowers who don't fit conventional agency underwriting boxes (self-employed, investor property, bank-statement income) but aren't necessarily lower credit quality.
asset_classes.market_size_issuance: Non-agency RMBS volume hit $192B through September 11, 2026, with $83B of that in non-QM - already a record for the category, beating all of 2025's $80B in just over 8 months. Non-QM has grown from a niche post-crisis product into a ~$200B market, with ~$100B of issuance expected this year, equivalent to roughly 7% of GSE gross issuance.
asset_classes.performance_commentary: Spreads have tightened materially: non-QM AAA tranches tightened to 123bp and AA to 140bp as of mid-September 2026 - real, sourced spread levels, not a proxy. Credit performance has also improved sharply year over year: 2026 YTD delinquency rates of 0.37% (prime) and 1.62% (non-QM) compare favorably to the stressed 2023 vintage, which saw 3.01% (prime) and 10.29% (non-QM) delinquencies surpass pre-pandemic highs.
asset_classes.institutional_commentary: Guggenheim Investments (Q3 2026 Structured Credit Outlook): non-agency RMBS borrowers 'skew toward the higher income cohort of the population with better credit scores' and are 'less sensitive to the stresses emerging in consumer credit' among lower-income borrowers - a favorable relative-credit-quality argument. Guggenheim's institutional positioning explicitly favors 'senior non-Agency RMBS securities' for income generation given 'favorable credit fundamentals, reduced interest-rate sensitivity, and appealing valuations.'
asset_classes.institutional_investment_activity: Guggenheim's Securitized Income ETF (GISC) and broader securitized-credit strategies carry active non-agency RMBS positioning per its Q2/Q3 2026 sector views. Angel Oak Mortgage Solutions - the leading non-QM originator - is targeting 50% year-over-year origination growth in 2026, funding continued record securitization volume (its Angel Oak Mortgage Trust program priced deals like AOMT 2026-3, a $279.6M non-prime RMBS, and AOMT 2026-5 at $228.2M in 2026 alone).
asset_classes.fed_sensitivity: Lower direct rate sensitivity than agency RMBS - Guggenheim specifically cites 'reduced interest-rate sensitivity' as part of the sector's appeal, partly because non-QM borrowers face 'structural disincentives to prepay' (many carry prepayment penalties or non-conforming rates that don't benefit as much from refinancing waves). The bigger Fed-linked risk runs through credit, not duration: if Fed policy tightens financial conditions enough to push unemployment higher, that's the historically dominant driver of RMBS delinquency spikes (the 2023 vintage stress was linked to 'an upward shift in the jobless rate'), not rate moves directly.
asset_classes.headwinds_tailwinds: Tailwind: record investor demand has tightened non-QM spreads meaningfully while credit performance has actually improved year over year - an unusually clean combination of rising volume, tightening spreads, and better fundamentals simultaneously. Headwind: 'fragmented non-QM origination and elevated 2026 supply could strain syndication capacity' - the same record issuance that signals strength could eventually outrun dealer/investor capacity to absorb it if the pace continues.
asset_classes.sentiment_outlook: Constructive and credit-differentiated from consumer credit broadly - the Guggenheim thesis (better-credit-quality borrowers, less exposed to the stress hitting lower-income consumers elsewhere) is a specific, falsifiable claim worth checking against future delinquency prints rather than a generic bullish view, and the current 0.37%/1.62% delinquency data supports it for now.
